client: I've been having a really hard time going to this café near my apartment — it's the place where my ex and I used to meet all the time, and every single time I walk in there, my heart just starts racing and I feel completely overwhelmed. It's gotten to the point where I've started avoiding it altogether, which is frustrating because it's honestly the most convenient spot for me to work from. I'm not totally sure talking about it is going to change how my body reacts, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: What you're describing — that rush of physical overwhelm the moment you step inside — makes complete sense, and it sounds genuinely exhausting to have a place that used to feel good now feel like something to brace against. Avoidance often brings short-term relief but can quietly shrink our world over time, which might be part of why it feels so frustrating. I'm really glad you decided to give this a shot, and I'm curious — when you imagine walking in there, what's the very first thought that tends to show up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, the first thought that shows up is something like "everyone's going to notice something's off about me" — like I walk in already convinced I'm being watched or judged. It's almost automatic, I don't even choose to think it, it just hits me before I've even taken my coat off. And then I feel this wave of shame on top of the anxiety, like I should be able to just be normal in my own workplace.
therapist: That automatic thought — "everyone can see something's wrong with me" — is such a classic example of what we call mind-reading, and it's striking how it arrives before you've even had a moment to settle in, almost like your brain is trying to protect you by scanning for danger first. And then that second layer of shame, the "I *should* be over this" — that one can be just as painful as the anxiety itself. I'm wondering, when that shame voice shows up and says you should just be normal, whose voice does it sound like to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That's a weird question to sit with, honestly. I think it sounds like... a mix of people, maybe my mom a little, but also just me? Like at some point I took over from whoever started it and now I'm the one saying it to myself constantly, which almost makes it worse because I can't even blame someone else for it.
therapist: That moment of recognition — "I took over and now *I'm* the one doing it" — is actually a really significant insight, even if it feels heavier right now rather than lighter. There's something almost lonely about that, like you inherited this critical voice and then lost the receipt, so you can't return it to anyone. I'm curious what it would feel like to think of that voice not as *you*, but as something you *learned* — something that made sense once but maybe doesn't have to have the last word anymore?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That image of losing the receipt actually kind of hit me, because yeah, there's no one left to give this back to. But when you say "it doesn't have to have the last word" — I don't know, it's been the loudest voice in my head for so long that I honestly can't picture what would fill that space if it quieted down. Part of me is almost scared of that, like without the criticism keeping me in check, what if I just... fall apart or stop trying altogether?
therapist: That fear — "what if the criticism is actually what's holding me together?" — is one of the most honest and courageous things a person can name, and it tells me that voice has convinced you it's load-bearing, like if you removed it the whole structure would collapse. But I'd gently offer this: what if the drive to try, to show up, to care — what if that was *yours* all along, and the critical voice just took credit for it? I'm wondering if you can think of even one time you did something meaningful or kept going, not because you criticized yourself into it, but because something else in you wanted to.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I want to believe that, I really do, but it's hard to separate the two when they've been tangled together for so long. Like, I can think of moments where I genuinely wanted something — I stayed up late finishing a project once because I was actually excited about it, not because I was terrified of failing. But almost immediately my brain goes, "yeah, but you only felt that way because you'd already beaten yourself up enough to get started," and I don't know how to argue back against that.
therapist: You just did something really important — you found the memory, you held it up, and even as your brain rushed in to reframe it, *you noticed that happening*, which is itself a form of arguing back. That critical voice is fast and well-practiced, but I want to stay with that late night for a moment — the excitement you felt before the voice swooped in to claim the credit, because that feeling was real and it was yours. What was the project?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It was a short story I'd been working on for weeks, this kind of weird, melancholy piece about a woman who keeps finding objects that belonged to people she never met. I remember finishing the last paragraph and just sitting there in the quiet, feeling like I'd actually made something real for once. But even saying that out loud right now, there's this pull to add "but it probably wasn't that good" — and I can feel it happening, like you said, but knowing it's there doesn't make it stop.
therapist: That story sounds genuinely beautiful — a woman finding traces of lives she never knew, there's something so tender and searching about that image, and I don't think it's a coincidence that *you* were the one who made it. And you just caught the voice mid-sentence, in real time, which is exactly the kind of awareness that starts to create a tiny bit of space between you and it — not enough to silence it yet, but enough to see it. I want to ask: in that quiet moment after you finished the last paragraph, before the voice arrived — what did that feeling in your chest actually feel like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It felt like... relief, I think, but also something fragile, like if I moved too fast it would break. There was this warmth in my chest, almost like I'd done something real for the first time in a long time. And then yeah, the voice came in and kind of flattened it, told me it wasn't enough, that one paragraph doesn't make me a writer.
therapist: That warmth, that fragile feeling — you described it so carefully, like you were almost protecting it even now just by putting words around it gently, and I think that tenderness *is* the thing the voice is most threatened by. It's striking that the voice didn't wait long — it came in right at the moment of something real, almost like it knew that warmth was dangerous somehow. I'm curious: what do you think the voice is actually afraid would happen if you let yourself just... stay in that feeling a little longer?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think... the voice is afraid that if I actually let myself feel that warmth, I'll want more of it, and then I'll have to face how little of it I actually have in my life. Like, it's almost safer to cut it off before I get attached to something I can't really hold onto. And that's a really uncomfortable thing to say out loud, because it makes the loneliness feel more real, not less.
therapist: What you just named is profound — that the voice isn't just cruel, it's *protective* in its own broken way, trying to shield you from wanting something and then grieving its absence. And saying it out loud didn't create the loneliness, it just let you finally see something that's been quietly there for a while, which takes real courage. I want to sit with you in that for a moment — because the fact that you *can* feel that warmth, even briefly, even when it gets cut short, tells me the capacity for it is still very much alive in you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually... lands differently than I expected it to. Like, I didn't think hearing someone else say it back to me would matter, but there's something about you calling it "the capacity is still alive" that makes me want to believe it, even though part of me immediately wants to push back and say "but what good is the capacity if I never actually use it." I guess I'm scared that knowing it's there just means there's more to lose.
therapist: That last line — "knowing it's there just means there's more to lose" — is one of the most honest things you've said today, and I think it points to something really important: that hope itself can feel like a risk when you've learned not to trust good things to stay. But I want to gently turn your own question back to you — you asked "what good is the capacity if I never use it," and I heard something in that, almost like a part of you is already imagining using it, already wondering what that could look like. What would "using it" even mean to you, in a life that felt a little more like that quiet moment after the last paragraph?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess "using it" would mean... letting myself actually look forward to something without immediately bracing for it to fall apart. Like, maybe making plans with someone and not spending the whole time waiting for them to cancel, or to get tired of me. But even saying that out loud feels dangerous, like I'm already setting myself up, and I don't know if I trust myself to handle it when it does go wrong.
therapist: What you just described — looking forward to something without the bracing, being with someone without the countdown to disappointment — that's not a small wish, that's a whole different way of moving through the world, and the fact that you could picture it means something. I notice there's a quiet tension in how you said it, like part of you really wants that and another part is already standing guard. I'm curious about that last piece — "I don't know if I trust myself to handle it when it goes wrong" — because I wonder if the fear isn't really about things going wrong, but about whether *you* will still be okay if they do?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
